items.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> leans on the left, tucked behind it a little <radical>cocoon</radical>, sealed tight. Nobody else knows it is there. You grew the crop in the open, then kept one seed back for yourself: <kanji>private</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Shi is the quiet one who keeps her own small field behind the house, and when anyone asks what she is growing in it she says 「<reading>し</reading>」 and closes the gate. Not rude, exactly. Whatever is in there is hers, and し is the only answer you are ever going to get.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は今コーヒーを飲みます。
example_sentences.english: I'm drinking coffee now.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は今[いま]コーヒーを飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは公園で遊びます。
example_sentences.english: We play in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は今日学校へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to school today.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は今日[きょう]学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: A single horizontal stroke is the ground floor: one.
items.meaning_mnemonic: One flat horizontal stroke with nothing else anywhere on the page is <kanji>one</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The talent show finally gets an audience: a sunburnt hiker named Itchy, with one mosquito bite right between his shoulder blades. He sits on the ground and scratches his back against the goat. Each scrape earns a groan of <reading>いち</reading>, いち, いち.
items.description: Beyond the plain counting number, 一 carries a wider sense of a single thing taken as a whole, so it turns up in words about being first, being the same, or doing something all at once. Write it as one confident horizontal stroke, left to right, and keep it flat and reasonably long — short or slanted, it starts to look like a fragment of some other character.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、友達と一緒に海に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I am going to the sea with a friend tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に海[うみ]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 朝ご飯にパンを一つ食べました。
example_sentences.english: I ate one piece of bread for breakfast.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]にパンを一[ひと]つ食[た]べました。

example_sentences.japanese: 水が一番安いです。
example_sentences.english: Water is the cheapest.
example_sentences.furigana: 水[みず]が一[いち]番[ばん]安[やす]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: Two stacked strokes count out two.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two flat strokes lie stacked, one over the other, with nothing else drawn. Simple as that: a plain, level <radical>two</radical>. Count the strokes and you already have the meaning — <kanji>two</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The waiter, Niko, stopped being surprised by raccoons years ago — now he just keeps score. He sets the second bowl beside the first, taps the table once, and says <reading>に</reading>, flat as a bell. It's how you announce a total, not a discovery. The raccoons snap chopsticks purely to hear him say it.
items.description: 二 is the plain counting two, used for quantities, dates, prices and floors. Its spoken form shifts with the counter that follows. The same character sounds different in a date than in a count of objects. Write it as two level horizontals, top to bottom, with the lower one clearly longer. That length difference is the whole character, and the two strokes never touch.

example_sentences.japanese: これを二つ買います。
example_sentences.english: I'll buy two of these.
example_sentences.furigana: これを二[ふた]つ買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 二日、犬と遊びました。

example_sentences.japanese: 二十日に彼女が来ます。

example_sentences.furigana: 二十[はつ]日[か]に彼[かの]女[じょ]が来[き]ます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> carries a <radical>big</radical> <radical>sheep</radical> on his back. It is too heavy, and he <radical>split</radical> it into pieces for everyone else. He never eats first, so this humble word means <kanji>me</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Boku is the errand boy who answers every question about who did it with the same word: 「<reading>ぼく</reading>」. Broke the gate? ぼく. Carried the sheep up the hill? ぼく. He never says his own name, so ぼく is the only name you have for him.

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は今日学校に行く。

example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]にパンを食[た]べる。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は公園で猫と遊ぶ。
example_sentences.english: I play with the cat at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は公[こう]園[えん]で猫[ねこ]と遊[あそ]ぶ。

items.mnemonic_text: Three stacked strokes: one, two, three.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and count what you see: <radical>three</radical> flat lines stacked neatly on top of each other. One line, then another, then a third. Three lines means, simply, <kanji>three</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful ranch hand named San lines up three fence rails on the mountain trail, tapping each one and calling out 「<reading>さん</reading>」 as she checks the count. Three rails, three, and San says the number every time.
items.description: The kanji for three, the number 3, appearing constantly in counting, dates, and prices.

example_sentences.japanese: 三時に起きます。
example_sentences.english: I wake up at three o'clock.
example_sentences.furigana: 三[さん]時[じ]に起[お]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: パンを三つ買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought three loaves of bread.
example_sentences.furigana: パンを三[みっ]つ買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: ここで三日待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I will wait here for three days.
example_sentences.furigana: ここで三[みっ]日[か]待[ま]ちます。

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth boxing in legs that kick four ways: four.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You peer into the closed box of the <radical>enclosure</radical>, walls all around, and inside you find a <radical>mouth</radical> trapped in the corner. It sits there counting on its lips, and the number it keeps landing on is four. An enclosure with a mouth inside: <kanji>four</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Inside those walls, a tiny shopkeeper named Shi is stacking exactly four onigiri and hissing "<reading>し</reading>, し, し" as she counts. Every time she runs out of breath, she's counted to four.
items.description: 四 and 西 are both boxes with strokes inside. 四 is a plain rectangle with two short strokes bending inward. 西 sits an extra horizontal bar above the box, which 四 never has.

example_sentences.japanese: パンを四つ買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought four pieces of bread.
example_sentences.furigana: パンを四[よっ]つ買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 四日に友達に会います。
example_sentences.english: I will meet my friend on the fourth.
example_sentences.furigana: 四[よっ]日[か]に友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]います。

example_sentences.japanese: これは四ですか？
example_sentences.english: Is this a four?
example_sentences.furigana: これは四[よん]ですか？

items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone grabs a <radical>broom</radical> and gives one <radical>slide</radical> across the <radical>ground</radical> to clear it. He opens his <radical>mouth</radical> and barks out tomorrow's orders. He is not the emperor, just the man everyone calls <kanji>mister</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kun is the teacher who refuses to use first names. Every boy in the class gets the same syllable barked after his surname — 「<reading>くん</reading>」 — as the seating chart comes out. Tanaka-くん. Sato-くん. It is how you know he means you.

example_sentences.japanese: 君は明日学校に行きますか。
example_sentences.english: Are you going to school tomorrow?
example_sentences.furigana: 君[きみ]は明日[あした]学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きますか。

items.mnemonic_text: A shape crossing itself, the hand held up: five fingers.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Two</radical> pairs of fingers and one more left over on the thumb comes to exactly <kanji>five</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The kid counting up his catch is Go, and once he hits five he throws his hands up and yells "<reading>ご</reading>!" like it's the winning number. Every time he lands a fifth thing, out comes that triumphant ご.
items.description: The kanji for five, the number 5, seen everywhere from prices and dates to counting and phone numbers.

example_sentences.japanese: パンを五つ買います。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、五時に学校へ行きます。

example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、五[ご]時[じ]に学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は五日待ちました。
example_sentences.english: He waited for five days.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は五[いつ]日[か]待[ま]ちました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> at the left edge, beside a hide hauled off in one sheet — all <radical>skin</radical>, no animal left. Someone walked past carrying it and is already down the road. That man you point at and cannot name: <kanji>he</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Hii is the little intake of breath you make when the man in the skin cloak goes past without a word — 「<reading>ひ</reading>」. By the time you finish it, he is round the corner. Every time you catch sight of him: ひ.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は今、公園にいます。
example_sentences.english: He's at the park right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は今[いま]、公[こう]園[えん]にいます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は今、コーヒーを飲みます。
example_sentences.english: She's drinking coffee now.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は今[いま]、コーヒーを飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は彼の家に来ました。
example_sentences.english: She came to his house.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は彼[かれ]の家[いえ]に来[き]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: A little hat on two legs stands over six.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the <radical>number eight</radical> standing tall, and then set a little <radical>lid</radical> right on top of it. That lid caps the eight and knocks it down two — from eight, you drop to six. The lid on top of eight always means <kanji>six</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A rock star climbs onto the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail and belts out six songs to the empty air. Every time he screams "<reading>ろく</reading>!" a cat appears, until six of them are yowling backup. That rock (ろく) show is how you hear six.
items.description: Means six; the basic number 6, seen everywhere from counting and prices to dates and times.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は今日六時に起きました。
example_sentences.english: I got up at six o'clock today.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は今日[きょう]六[ろく]時[じ]に起[お]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋にパンが六つあります。
example_sentences.english: There are six pieces of bread in this room.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]にパンが六[むっ]つあります。

example_sentences.japanese: 六日に友達と映画を見ます。

example_sentences.furigana: 六[むい]日[か]に友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

items.mnemonic_text: A slanted cross like a scythe cutting seven.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>One</radical> stroke and a <radical>second</radical> one bent back on itself is how you get all the way to <kanji>seven</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A shy cat at Grandma Kane's shrine will only come out when you call it exactly seven times — and each time you call, you shush the other cats: <reading>しち</reading>, しち, quiet now. By the seventh しち, it finally pads down the mossy steps.
items.description: 七 and 十 are both a bar crossed by a second stroke. 十 keeps that stroke straight, running top to bottom. 七 bends it: it drops, curves right, and flicks upward at the end.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は七日に学校へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to school on the seventh.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は七[なな]日[にち]に学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、パンを七つ買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought seven pieces of bread today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、パンを七[なな]つ買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、七時に起きます。
example_sentences.english: I will wake up at seven o'clock tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、七[なな]時[じ]に起[お]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: Two strokes spreading apart like the number eight opening up.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two strokes leaning apart from one point, splitting cleanly down the middle, is <kanji>eight</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A honeybee — a <reading>はち</reading> in Japanese — drifts down to the onigiri shelf in Koichi's konbini and lands on exactly eight of them, one after another. You count the buzzing little はち as it goes: eight stops, eight onigiri.
items.description: The same two falling strokes, arranged three ways. 八 leaves a clear gap at the top with both strokes leaning apart. 人 joins them into one peak. 入 tucks the short stroke under the long one so the top overhangs.

example_sentences.japanese: ここに八を書きます。
example_sentences.english: I will write an eight here.
example_sentences.furigana: ここに八[はち]を書[か]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、パンを八つ買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought eight pieces of bread yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、パンを八[やっ]つ買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 八日に友達と会います。
example_sentences.english: I'm meeting a friend on the eighth.
example_sentences.furigana: 八[よう]日[か]に友[とも]達[だち]と会[あ]います。

items.mnemonic_text: A hook curling back at the top of the count: nine.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character as a hook curling forward — the cane you lean on after a long day. Count the mountain trail's switchbacks, one by one, up to the very last, most brutal bend. That bend curls exactly like this hook. Lean your cane there: that's <kanji>nine</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At bend nine on the mountain trail, you finally reach the vending machine. Your legs give out — you go "<reading>きゅう</reading>!" and collapse against it. That sharp cry of relief at spot nine is きゅう.
items.description: 九 and 力 are both two strokes with a hook, hooking opposite ways. 九 opens with a short slash, then a stroke that curves right and flicks upward. 力 opens with a flat horizontal that turns down and hooks to the left, with a slash cutting through it.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、パンを九つ買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought nine pieces of bread yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、パンを九[ここの]つ買[か]いました。

example_sentences.english: Nine students came today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、学[がく]生[せい]が九[きゅう]人[にん]来[き]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: ここで彼を九日待ちました。
example_sentences.english: I waited for him here for nine days.
example_sentences.furigana: ここで彼[かれ]を九[ここの]日[か]待[ま]ちました。

items.mnemonic_text: A perfect plus sign, fingers of both hands: ten.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two strokes crossing at dead centre with four arms of equal length is <kanji>ten</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A judo champion bursts into Koichi's konbini and slaps down exactly ten coins on the beeping till, shouting <reading>じゅう</reading> with each one. Every time you picture that plus-sign cross, hear the judo master's じゅう ringing out.
items.description: 十 is a plain cross: one flat horizontal and one straight vertical. 千 adds a slanting flick above the bar. 七 bends the second stroke instead, curving it right and flicking upward at the end rather than running straight down.

example_sentences.japanese: これを十買います。
example_sentences.english: I will buy ten of these.
example_sentences.furigana: これを十[じゅう]買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 十日に家へ帰ります。
example_sentences.english: I will go home on the 10th.
example_sentences.furigana: 十[とお]日[か]に家[いえ]へ帰[かえ]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 一から十まで書きます。
example_sentences.english: I will write from one to ten.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いち]から十[じゅう]まで書[か]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: One (一) over a white (白) sheet counted a hundred times.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>one</radical> stroke sits on top of a blinding <radical>white</radical> light bulb. The light is so bright the stroke multiplies into copies of itself. Soon there are exactly a <kanji>hundred</kanji> strokes glowing on the ceiling.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a hiccuping cook keeps counting onigiri. Every time he hits a full tray, he lets out a huge "<reading>ひゃく</reading>!" — a hiccup and a yell in one. A hundred rice balls is a lot to hiccup through.
items.description: 百 is 白 with one extra stroke on top. 白 caps its box with a small flick; 百 turns that cap into a full-width horizontal bar.

example_sentences.japanese: 一から百まで書きました。
example_sentences.english: I wrote from one to one hundred.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いち]から百[ひゃく]まで書[か]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 学生が百人来ました。
example_sentences.english: A hundred students came.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]が百[ひゃく]人[にん]来[き]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 本を百買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a hundred books.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]を百[ひゃく]買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A slash over ten (十) multiplies it into a thousand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You draw a big <radical>ten</radical> cross on a market sign, then slash one more line down through its top corner. That extra cut bends the sign until it reads a much bigger number. Now the sign advertises rice for one <kanji>thousand</kanji> coins.
items.reading_mnemonic: A senator named Sen shows up at the shrine and drops a thousand coins into the offering box all at once. "That's from all my constituents," she says, "<reading>せん</reading> of them exactly." Every time you see this kanji, hear Sen bragging about her せん coins.
items.description: Count the horizontals and look at the top. 千 has one bar under a slanting flick. 十 has one bar and no flick, just a straight cross. 午 and 干 both carry two bars — 午 under a flick, 干 starting flat.

example_sentences.japanese: 一から千まで書きました。
example_sentences.english: I wrote from one to one thousand.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いち]から千[せん]まで書[か]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 学生が千人来ました。
example_sentences.english: A thousand students came.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]が千[せん]人[にん]来[き]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 千の魚を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw a thousand fish.
example_sentences.furigana: 千[せん]の魚[さかな]を見[み]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: A single hooked mark standing for a whole ten thousand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A single banner flaps above a busy market stall. The vendor scrawls one more zero on it every time a customer buys something. By nightfall the banner is crammed with exactly <kanji>ten thousand</kanji> zeros.
items.reading_mnemonic: A street vendor named Manny throws his arms wide under that banner and yells, "Man, I've sold ten thousand of these!" You can hear the <reading>まん</reading> right there in his ecstatic "Man!" as the crowd surges in.
items.description: 万 and 方 share a horizontal over a hooked stroke. 万 is just those two: a flat bar, then a stroke that drops and hooks left. 方 adds a dot on top and a short slash, so it runs to four strokes against 万's three.

example_sentences.japanese: 一から万まで書きます。
example_sentences.english: I'll write from one to ten thousand.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いち]から万[まん]まで書[か]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 学生が一万人来ました。
example_sentences.english: Ten thousand students came.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がく]生[せい]が一[いち]万[まん]人[にん]来[き]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 一万の本があります。
example_sentences.english: There are ten thousand books.
example_sentences.furigana: 一[いち]万[まん]の本[ほん]があります。

items.mnemonic_text: A boxed shape holding the round yen coin.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A stray coin rolls into a <radical>wide box</radical> with no lid. It spins in loops all night and rubs its edges perfectly smooth. By morning it is a shiny <kanji>circle</kanji> of yen.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the beeping till spits out change, and a friend named En scoops up every round coin, grinning "these <reading>えん</reading> are mine." Every time you hear the till beep, picture En pocketing えん.
items.description: Means yen (Japan's currency) and also circle or round; shows up on money, prices, and words for round shapes.

example_sentences.japanese: この本は千円でした。
example_sentences.english: This book was a thousand yen.
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]は千[せん]円[えん]でした。

example_sentences.japanese: コーヒーは三百円で、安いです。
example_sentences.english: The coffee is three hundred yen, and cheap.
example_sentences.furigana: コーヒーは三[さん]百[びゃく]円[えん]で、安[やす]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: あの映画は千五百円で、高いです。
example_sentences.english: That movie is fifteen hundred yen, which is expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: あの映[えい]画[が]は千[せん]五[ご]百[ひゃく]円[えん]で、高[たか]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: A window with a line: the sun rising to mark the day.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A box with one bar straight through the middle is the <kanji>sun</kanji>, logged once and then once again.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat wakes at dawn and greets the rising sun with the same cry every morning: "<reading>にち</reading>! にち!" The others answer, and that's how the whole shrine knows a new day has started.
items.description: Check the top and count the bars. 日 is a plain box with one horizontal inside. 白 is the same box with a small flick added on top. 目 has no cap but carries two horizontals instead of one.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: Today I'm watching a movie with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日日本語を話します。
example_sentences.english: I speak Japanese every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]日本[にほん]語[ご]を話[はな]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 日曜日に海へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: On Sunday I'm going to the sea.
example_sentences.furigana: 日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]に海[うみ]へ行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: A crescent with two lines: the moon marking each month.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A thin crescent with two lines drawn across its middle is the <kanji>moon</kanji> half hidden behind cloud.
items.reading_mnemonic: A gecko has claimed the moon as its own, scuttling across the crescent every night. Whenever it does, you hear its little feet go <reading>げつ</reading>, げつ against the pale surface. That gecko-on-the-moon sound is how you remember げつ.
items.description: Means moon or month; a common kanji that shows up in dates, days of the week (Monday), and countless month-related words.

example_sentences.japanese: 来月、友達に会います。
example_sentences.english: I'll meet a friend next month.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]月[げつ]、友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 今、月を見ています。
example_sentences.english: I'm looking at the moon right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]、月[つき]を見[み]ています。

example_sentences.japanese: 月曜日に学校へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school on Monday.
example_sentences.furigana: 月[げつ]曜[よう]日[ひ]に学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: A person with sparks flying off each side: fire.
items.meaning_mnemonic: One figure with sparks flying off both shoulders is standing far too close to the <kanji>fire</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line and lets out a puff of flame with a raspy caw: 「<reading>か</reading>!」. The flame and the sound arrive together, so when you see this fire kanji, you hear Kaa's か.

example_sentences.japanese: 火曜日に友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: On Tuesday I'm watching a movie with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 火[か]曜[よう]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 来週の火曜日はとても忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: Next Tuesday I'm really busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]の火[か]曜[よう]日[ひ]はとても忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 火曜日の朝、公園に行きます。
example_sentences.english: Tuesday morning, I'm going to the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 火[か]曜[よう]日[ひ]の朝[あさ]、公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: Streams splashing out from a central flow: water.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You stand at a riverbank while <radical>water</radical> splashes out in every direction and soaks your face. The wild branching spray freezes into that jagged shape of <kanji>water</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank a swimmer named Sui dives in and shouts "<reading>すい</reading>!" as the cold hits, then keeps splashing everyone within reach. Every time you see this kanji, hear Sui hollering すい from the water.

example_sentences.japanese: 暑いから、水を飲みます。
example_sentences.english: It's hot, so I'll drink some water.
example_sentences.furigana: 暑[あつ]いから、水[みず]を飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 水曜日に友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: On Wednesday I'll watch a movie with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 水[すい]曜[よう]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝、水を飲みます。
example_sentences.english: Every morning I drink water.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]、水[みず]を飲[の]みます。

items.mnemonic_text: A trunk with roots and branches: a tree.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A straight <radical>tree</radical> trunk shoots up with roots digging into the dirt and branches spreading wide on top. Roots below and branches above, this whole shape is a <kanji>tree</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki, the tree spirit, giggles as she climbs to the very top and peeks over the leaves — she's playing "<reading>もく</reading>" (peekaboo), disappearing behind branches every time the wind blows. Whenever you spot this tree, hear her whisper もく from up in the canopy.
items.description: 木 is the bare tree: a horizontal, a vertical, and two strokes sweeping down from the crossing. 本 is exactly this plus one short horizontal laid across the lower trunk.

example_sentences.japanese: 木曜日に友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: On Thursday I'm watching a movie with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 木[もく]曜[よう]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: あの木はとても高いです。
example_sentences.english: That tree over there is really tall.
example_sentences.furigana: あの木[き]はとても高[たか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎週木曜日に学校へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school every Thursday.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]週[しゅう]木[もく]曜[よう]日[ひ]に学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: A roof over a mountain of buried gold and money.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Split</radical> the <radical>king</radical>'s hoard, <radical>put together</radical> every <radical>single item</radical> of it again, and it is all still <kanji>gold</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane keeps her real fortune under the shrine's giant bell, and every time a cat brushes it, it goes <reading>きん</reading>. That soft きん ring is the sound of gold sitting safe underneath.

example_sentences.japanese: 金曜日に友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: On Friday I'll watch a movie with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 金[きん]曜[よう]日[ひ]に友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: お金がないから、今日は家に帰ります。
example_sentences.english: I don't have any money, so I'm going home today.
example_sentences.furigana: お金[かね]がないから、今日[きょう]は家[いえ]に帰[かえ]ります。

example_sentences.japanese: 現金でご飯を買います。
example_sentences.english: I'll pay for the meal in cash.
example_sentences.furigana: 現[げん]金[きん]でご飯[はん]を買[か]います。

items.mnemonic_text: A cross pushed into the ground: earth and soil.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A cross planted firmly on one flat line is a marker driven into open <kanji>soil</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A gardener drops to his knees in the plot and starts digging with his bare hands, going "do, do, do" (<reading>ど</reading>) as he flings soil over his shoulder. Every heavy handful he tosses out lands with that same low ど grunt.

example_sentences.japanese: 土曜日に公園へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I'm going to the park on Saturday.
example_sentences.furigana: 土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]に公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎週土曜日に海へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to the sea every Saturday.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]週[しゅう]土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]に海[うみ]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今週の土曜日は忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: I am busy this Saturday.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[こん]週[しゅう]の土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]は忙[いそが]しいです。

items.mnemonic_text: Three peaks rising up: a mountain range.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Three peaks on one base line with the middle one highest is a <kanji>mountain</kanji> range drawn in four strokes.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, the lone vending machine has a face, and it greets every exhausted hiker like an old friend: "You made it — welcome, san (<reading>さん</reading>)!" It calls everyone さん because on this mountain, reaching the peak earns you respect.
items.description: Means "mountain"; a common N5 kanji seen in nature words and countless place and family names.

example_sentences.japanese: あの山は高いです。
example_sentences.english: That mountain is high.
example_sentences.furigana: あの山[やま]は高[たか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 週末、友達と山に行きました。
example_sentences.english: I went to the mountains with a friend on the weekend.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]、友[とも]達[だち]と山[やま]に行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 山の写真はどこですか。
example_sentences.english: Where is the photo of the mountain?
example_sentences.furigana: 山[やま]の写[しゃ]真[しん]はどこですか。

items.mnemonic_text: Three flowing lines of a running river.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Three thin <radical>river</radical> lines trickle down a mountainside side by side. A storm swells all three until they touch and merge together. Merged into one, they roar as a single wide <kanji>river</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank you meet a fisherman who has cast a line into every one of those three currents. He grins and tells you he's caught a thousand — <reading>せん</reading> — fish today, one for each ripple in the river.
items.description: Means "river"; a common N5 kanji seen in nature words and countless place names.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、川に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I am going to the river today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、川[かわ]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、友達と一緒に川で遊びました。
example_sentences.english: I played by the river with my friend yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に川[かわ]で遊[あそ]びました。

example_sentences.japanese: 川で魚を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw a fish in the river.
example_sentences.furigana: 川[かわ]で魚[さかな]を見[み]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: A person (大) with a line above their head: the heavens.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A giant pulls up the flat <radical>ground</radical> from under your feet like a bedsheet. He drapes it high over your head instead. Now the ground covers the whole world as the <kanji>sky</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tent-pitcher hikes to the top of the mountain trail and, instead of camping on the ground, throws a giant tent (<reading>てん</reading>) up into the air to sleep among the clouds. When you crane your neck at the sky, you spot that tent (てん) floating right there in heaven.
items.description: 天 is 大 with an extra horizontal laid across the top, above the outstretched arms. 大 has one horizontal, 天 has two.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日はいい天気ですね。
example_sentences.english: The weather is nice today, isn't it?
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]はいい天[てん]気[き]ですね。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は天気がいいですか。
example_sentences.english: Will the weather be nice tomorrow?
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は天[てん]気[き]がいいですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日は天気が良かったです。
example_sentences.english: The weather was good yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]は天[てん]気[き]が良[よ]かったです。

items.mnemonic_text: Steam rising with an X inside: the invisible energy or mood.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Steam</radical> lifting off a field somebody has just had to <radical>mow</radical> is the <kanji>spirit</kanji> leaving the grass.
items.reading_mnemonic: The steam curls up and out pops Kiki, the tree spirit, giggling as the wind stirs her branches. She rides that rising energy on a breeze of 「<reading>き</reading>」.
items.description: Means spirit or energy; a very common kanji found in words about mood, feeling, weather, and vitality.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は元気ですか。
example_sentences.english: Are you feeling well today?
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は元[げん]気[き]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の犬は病気です。
example_sentences.english: My dog is sick.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の犬[いぬ]は病[びょう]気[き]です。

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋は気持ちがいいです。
example_sentences.english: This room feels nice.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]は気[き]持[も]ちがいいです。

items.mnemonic_text: Grass on top of a person changing (化): a blooming flower.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A tuft of <radical>grass</radical> gets tired of being trampled every day. It shoots one blade straight up and pops a bright bloom on top. Now people step around it, admiring the new <kanji>flower</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, lands right in the middle of the flowerbed and lets out a proud 「<reading>か</reading>」, singeing every petal within reach. Now the only flower left standing is the scorched one under her claws.
items.description: Means "flower"; a very common everyday kanji seen in words for flowers, plants, and blossoms.

example_sentences.japanese: 母に花を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought flowers for my mother.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]に花[はな]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 公園で花を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw flowers at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 公[こう]園[えん]で花[はな]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: この花は高いです。
example_sentences.english: This flower is expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: この花[はな]は高[たか]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Words</radical> stand on the left, on the right an <radical>old bird</radical> with its head cocked, waiting. You have talked for ten minutes and the bird still cannot tell which person you mean. It asks the only question left: <kanji>who</kanji>?
items.reading_mnemonic: Sui is the owl who works the gate. She leans down, blinks once, and hoots 「<reading>すい</reading>」, which in owl means name, please. Nobody gets past her without answering it. すい, すい, until you say who you are.

example_sentences.japanese: 誰が先生ですか。
example_sentences.english: Who is the teacher?
example_sentences.furigana: 誰[だれ]が先[せん]生[せい]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: この料理は誰でも作れます。
example_sentences.english: Anyone can make this dish.
example_sentences.furigana: この料[りょう]理[り]は誰[だれ]でも作[つく]れます。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋には誰もいませんでした。
example_sentences.english: There was no one in the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]には誰[だれ]もいませんでした。

items.mnemonic_text: A mark sitting on top of a line: up and above.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>divination</radical> stick standing upright on <radical>one</radical> flat line points at everything <kanji>above</kanji> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful mountaineer plants her flag at the summit and shouts "Joe!" as she looks up at the sky — <reading>じょう</reading> rings out across the peak. Every time you look up and above you, you hear her じょう echoing back down.
items.description: Means "up" or "above"; a very common N5 kanji appearing in words for direction, position, and going up.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生は話すのが上手です。
example_sentences.english: The teacher is good at speaking.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]は話[はな]すのが上手[じょうず]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 本の上に猫が寝ています。
example_sentences.english: A cat is sleeping on the book.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]の上[うえ]に猫[ねこ]が寝[ね]ています。

example_sentences.japanese: 手を上げてください。
example_sentences.english: Please raise your hand.
example_sentences.furigana: 手[て]を上[あ]げてください。

items.mnemonic_text: A mark hanging under a line: down and below.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Divination</radical> marks scratched underneath <radical>one</radical> flat line are all pointing <kanji>below</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, dives straight down off the power line and lets out a sharp 「<reading>か</reading>」 as she plummets toward the ground below. Every time she drops down, that same caw of 「か」 rings out.
items.description: Means down or below; a very common kanji appearing in words about lower position, direction, and going down.

example_sentences.japanese: 本はあの窓の下です。
example_sentences.english: The book is under that window.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]はあの窓[まど]の下[した]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日地下鉄で学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school by subway every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]地[ち]下[か]鉄[てつ]で学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 僕は話すのが下手です。
example_sentences.english: I'm not good at speaking.
example_sentences.furigana: 僕[ぼく]は話[はな]すのが下手[へた]です。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> stands at the left with a line in hand — a <radical>barb</radical> at its end, a bar of <radical>ground</radical> above the open <radical>mouth</radical>. He hauls something up, stares, mouth open, no idea <kanji>what</kanji> it is.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow drops onto the power line above him and looks at the thing on the hook. She has never seen one either. All she manages is one puzzled croak — 「<reading>か</reading>?」 — with a little puff of flame behind it. か? か? Neither of them knows.

example_sentences.japanese: これは何ですか。
example_sentences.english: What is this?
example_sentences.furigana: これは何[なに]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 今、何時ですか。
example_sentences.english: What time is it now?
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]、何[なん]時[じ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 朝ご飯に何を食べますか。
example_sentences.english: What will you eat for breakfast?
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]に何[なに]を食[た]べますか。

items.mnemonic_text: A box speared straight through the middle.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>mouth</radical>, that open square, and now imagine a single spear driven straight down through its center. The line splits the opening into two even halves, landing dead in the middle. Whatever you skewer that cleanly is right in the <kanji>middle</kanji>, tucked inside.
items.reading_mnemonic: Chuu, the loyal mouse, refuses to guard the door or the back — he plants himself squarely in the <reading>ちゅう</reading>, the very middle of the room, so no threat can slip past on either side. "The center is where a loyal mouse belongs," he squeaks.
items.description: Means middle or inside; extremely common, appearing in words about being in the middle of doing something, insides, and locations like the center of town.

example_sentences.japanese: みんな、中に入りました。
example_sentences.english: Everyone went inside.
example_sentences.furigana: みんな、中[なか]に入[はい]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋の真ん中に座りました。
example_sentences.english: I sat in the middle of the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]の真[ま]ん中[なか]に座[すわ]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 家の中で本を読みました。
example_sentences.english: I read a book inside the house.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[いえ]の中[なか]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みました。

items.mnemonic_text: A person stretching arms and legs out wide: big.
items.meaning_mnemonic: One figure with both arms flung as wide as they go and the legs to match is simply <kanji>big</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The person is stretching so wide because they're measuring Dai, the giant baby, who is the size of a truck. You gasp <reading>だい</reading> as he cries an earthquake and you realize nothing has ever been this big.
items.description: All four share the same spread-armed figure. 大 is the bare shape. 太 adds a dot underneath, 犬 adds a dot at the top right, and 天 caps it with an extra horizontal above the arms. If nothing has been added, it is 大.

example_sentences.japanese: その犬は大きいです。
example_sentences.english: That dog is big.
example_sentences.furigana: その犬[いぬ]は大[おお]きいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、大学に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I am going to the university tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、大[だい]学[がく]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: お母さんは大丈夫ですか。
example_sentences.english: Is your mother okay?
example_sentences.furigana: お母[かあ]さんは大[だい]丈[じょう]夫[ぶ]ですか。

items.mnemonic_text: A tiny hook with two small dots: small.
items.meaning_mnemonic: One upright with a tiny stroke either side of it, both barely there at all, is <kanji>small</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sho, the tiny stage magician, snaps his white glove and shrinks the whole set until the doves look like specks. As everything gets impossibly small, the crowd gasps, "<reading>しょう</reading>!" — the man himself is the smallest thing on stage.
items.description: 小 is three strokes: a hooked vertical with a short dash on each side. 少 is 小 with a fourth stroke, a slash sweeping down to the left beneath it. If there is a tail, it is 少.

example_sentences.japanese: あの小さい猫を見ましたか。
example_sentences.english: Did you see that small cat?
example_sentences.furigana: あの小[ちい]さい猫[ねこ]を見[み]ましたか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の部屋は小さいです。
example_sentences.english: My room is small.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の部屋[へや]は小[ちい]さいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、小さい本を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a small book yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、小[ちい]さい本[ほん]を買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A hand over a craftsman's tool, held in the left hand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The hand that holds the <radical>construction</radical> ruler steady while the other one works is your <kanji>left</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A samurai marches into Koichi's konbini and slams down a coin with his left hand, barking "<reading>さ</reading>!" as he demands the last onigiri. Every time you see this kanji, hear that samurai's sharp さ ringing off the beeping till.
items.description: Means "left," the opposite of right; shows up constantly in directions and in the compound 左右 (left and right).

example_sentences.japanese: 駅は左です。
example_sentences.english: The station is on the left.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]は左[ひだり]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 左に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go left.
example_sentences.furigana: 左[ひだり]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 左の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I will open the left window.
example_sentences.furigana: 左[ひだり]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

items.mnemonic_text: A hand over a mouth, the right hand that feeds you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You balance a flat slab of <radical>ground</radical> just above your <radical>mouth</radical>, ready to catch crumbs falling from it. Only one hand is steady enough to hold it there. That steady hand is your <kanji>right</kanji> hand.
items.reading_mnemonic: You reach for the last onigiri on Koichi's shelf with your right hand and your fingers close on nothing but air, so you let out a soft "<reading>う</reading>う" of disappointment. That little "うう" is the sound you make when your right hand comes up empty.
items.description: 右, 左 and 石 all park something under a two-stroke top. 右 and 左 differ in what sits below: 右 has a small box, 左 a short cross-like piece. 石 shares 右's box but writes the top as a cliff, the horizontal running along the top with only its left end turning down.

example_sentences.japanese: トイレは右です。
example_sentences.english: The toilet is on the right.
example_sentences.furigana: トイレは右[みぎ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: ここから右に行きます。
example_sentences.english: We will go right from here.
example_sentences.furigana: ここから右[みぎ]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 右の部屋で寝ます。
example_sentences.english: I sleep in the room on the right.
example_sentences.furigana: 右[みぎ]の部屋[へや]で寝[ね]ます。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) tangled in a tree (木): sunrise in the east.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the <radical>sun</radical> rising and getting tangled in the branches of a <radical>tree</radical> on the horizon. You see the sun caught right behind that tree first thing in the morning — and the sun always comes up in the east. Sun plus tree, hung together at dawn: that's <kanji>east</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker faces the sunrise and lets out a long, tired yawn — a huge "<reading>とう</reading>" that echoes down the slope. Every morning she climbs to greet the east with that same sleepy とう.

example_sentences.japanese: 東の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I open the east window.
example_sentences.furigana: 東[ひがし]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の東で友達に会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met a friend east of the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の東[ひがし]で友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの町は東です。
example_sentences.english: That town is to the east.
example_sentences.furigana: あの町[まち]は東[ひがし]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A bird settling into its nest as the sun sets in the west.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A frame with two legs coming out of the bottom is the sun sinking behind a fence in the <kanji>west</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the star student, insists she always knows exactly where the sun sets. She marches to the western edge of the sports field at dusk and points. She calls out 「<reading>せい</reading>, that way!」 while the whole class watches the sky turn orange behind her.
items.description: 西 and 四 are both boxes with strokes inside. 四 is a plain rectangle with two short legs bending inward. 西 sits an extra horizontal bar across the very top, above the box, which 四 never has.

example_sentences.japanese: 学校は町の西です。
example_sentences.english: The school is in the west of the town.
example_sentences.furigana: 学[がっ]校[こう]は町[まち]の西[にし]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は西から来ました。
example_sentences.english: He came from the west.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は西[にし]から来[き]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは一緒に西へ行きました。
example_sentences.english: We went west together.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは一[いっ]緒[しょ]に西[にし]へ行[い]きました。

items.mnemonic_text: A warm shelter facing the sunny south.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Somebody upends a <radical>wide box</radical> on the hot sand. Across its flat top, two matchsticks lie laid in a <radical>cross</radical>, like the world's worst weather vane. A flamingo nudges the box round and round all afternoon. Whichever arm ends up warmest — that one points <kanji>south</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A backpacker named Nan has been hiking down the mountain trail for days, always heading south toward warmer weather. Every time someone asks which way she's going, she just points and sighs, "<reading>なん</reading>... south, always south." The word なん sticks because Nan won't stop saying it.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の南は海です。
example_sentences.english: South of the station is the sea.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の南[みなみ]は海[うみ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 私は南の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I will open the south window.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は南[みなみ]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は南から来ました。
example_sentences.english: He came from the south.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は南[みなみ]から来[き]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: Two people back to back turning away from the cold north.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two people stand back to back with a <radical>spoon</radical> each, both refusing to face the wind coming down from the <kanji>north</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Up on the mountain trail, the wind off the northern peak is so brutal that a hiker named Hoku pulls his hood tight and mutters "<reading>ほく</reading>, ほく" through chattering teeth as he trudges. Hear him — ほく — every time you point north.

example_sentences.japanese: 北は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It is cold in the north.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]は寒[さむ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 北から来ました。
example_sentences.english: I came from the north.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]から来[き]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 北の窓を開けます。
example_sentences.english: I will open the north window.
example_sentences.furigana: 北[きた]の窓[まど]を開[あ]けます。

items.mnemonic_text: Evening (夕) plus divination: reading fortunes outside.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Divination</radical> done in the <radical>evening</radical> has to be done <kanji>outside</kanji>, where the stars can be seen.
items.reading_mnemonic: You lock yourself out of Koichi's konbini after hours and a guy named Guy comes tapping the glass from the cold, calling "<reading>がい</reading>! I'm still stuck out here!" He is very much on the outside.
items.description: Means "outside"; a common N5 kanji appearing in words for the outdoors and things that are external.

example_sentences.japanese: 来年、外国に行きます。
example_sentences.english: Next year, I will go to a foreign country.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]、外[がい]国[こく]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: あの人は外国人ですか。
example_sentences.english: Is that person a foreigner?
example_sentences.furigana: あの人[ひと]は外[がい]国[こく]人[じん]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、外は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It is cold outside today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、外[そと]は寒[さむ]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: A blade cutting the way forward, in front of you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>knife</radical> sharp enough to <radical>split</radical> the <radical>moon</radical> gets carried out in <kanji>front</kanji> where everybody can see it.
items.reading_mnemonic: A calm Zen monk stands out front of the shop, arriving before everyone else, and he bows and murmurs <reading>ぜん</reading> as he settles into place. He's always in ぜん — front and center, before the doors open.
items.description: Means front or before; extremely common in words for physical position (in front of) and time (before, previous), such as before an event or the front of a building.

example_sentences.japanese: ここに名前を書きます。
example_sentences.english: I will write my name here.
example_sentences.furigana: ここに名[な]前[まえ]を書[か]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日の午前、病院へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to the hospital tomorrow morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]の午[ご]前[ぜん]、病[びょう]院[いん]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の前で友達を待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I will wait for my friend in front of the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の前[まえ]で友[とも]達[だち]を待[ま]ちます。

items.mnemonic_text: A small step trailing behind: after and behind.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A short <radical>step</radical>, one <radical>tiny thread</radical> of a path and a <radical>trailing foot</radical> leaves you well <kanji>after</kanji> everybody else.
items.reading_mnemonic: The trailing runner finally staggers across the finish line, dead last, and gasps out a weak "<reading>ご</reading>... ご..." — trying to say "go" but only managing to arrive after everyone else. That breathless ご is the sound that lands whenever this kanji shows up.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の後ろで待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I will wait behind the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の後[うし]ろで待[ま]ちます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日の午後、図書館に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to the library this afternoon.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]の午[ご]後[ご]、図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: これが最後のお菓子です。
example_sentences.english: This is the last snack.
example_sentences.furigana: これが最[さい]後[ご]のお菓[か]子[し]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A marker at the top of the day: noon.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a sundial standing on the <radical>ground</radical> — that flat line is the earth beneath it. A pole rises up from the ground. At the top of the day, its shadow points straight down and vanishes onto that line. No shadow at all: that's exactly <kanji>noon</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At high noon a golfer named Gordon lines up his shot and yells "<reading>ご</reading>!" as he swings, because he can't wait until the sun drops. His voice echoes across the empty midday field: ご, ご, ご.
items.description: All three are bars on a vertical under a slanting flick. 午 has two bars and its vertical stops at the upper one. 牛 also has two, but its vertical pushes up above the top bar. 千 has only one bar.

example_sentences.japanese: 午前は学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school in the morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 午[ご]前[ぜん]は学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 午後は映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I will watch a movie in the afternoon.
example_sentences.furigana: 午[ご]後[ご]は映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日の午前、友達に会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met a friend yesterday morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]の午[ご]前[ぜん]、友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A tree (木) with a line marking its root: the origin, a book.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>tree</radical> standing tall, with the <radical>ground</radical> drawn as one flat line across its trunk — right where the roots meet the soil. That line marks the tree's own origin. Press pages flat from that origin, and you have a <kanji>book</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A monk named <reading>ほん</reading> sits on the mossy steps at Grandma Kane's shrine, reading the same book over and over. Every time a cat brushes past, he mutters "ほん, ほん" without looking up — he cannot put that book down.
items.description: 本 is 木 with one extra stroke: a short horizontal laid across the lower trunk. Nothing else changes, so that little bar down at the base is the only thing to look for.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: I read a book every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日本[にほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 来年、日本に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to Japan next year.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]、日本[にほん]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日はペンを三本買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought three pens yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]はペンを三[さん]本[ぼん]買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: Two legs walking: a person.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two legs meeting at the top with nothing whatsoever holding them up is the entire shape of a <kanji>person</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Jin, the friendly giant, is the biggest person you'll ever meet, ducking through every doorway just to say hello. When you spot this character, picture him waving down at you and hear the giant himself: <reading>じん</reading>.
items.description: 人 is the two-stroke figure that meets at a single clean peak. 入 slides its short stroke down the long one so the top overhangs, and 八 keeps the two strokes apart with a gap between them.

example_sentences.japanese: あの人は誰ですか。
example_sentences.english: Who is that person over there?
example_sentences.furigana: あの人[ひと]は誰[だれ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の友達は外国人です。
example_sentences.english: My friend is a foreigner.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の友[とも]達[だち]は外[がい]国[こく]人[じん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は一人で帰ります。
example_sentences.english: I will go home alone today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は一人[ひとり]で帰[かえ]ります。

items.mnemonic_text: A figure kneeling gracefully: a woman.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at the character and you'll see a <radical>woman</radical> kneeling gracefully, one arm sweeping across, the other resting low. That elegant kneeling pose is exactly how you were taught to spot a <kanji>woman</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A woman named Jo sweeps into Koichi's konbini and orders in a booming voice, "<reading>じょ</reading>, that's me!" The whole shelf of onigiri rattles as she says it, so じょ is stuck to this woman for good.
items.description: Means "woman"; a very common N5 kanji that appears in words for females and in compounds relating to girls and women.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女と一緒に映画館へ行きました。
example_sentences.english: I went to the cinema with my girlfriend.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]館[かん]へ行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの女の人は誰ですか。
example_sentences.english: Who is that woman?
example_sentences.furigana: あの女[おんな]の人[ひと]は誰[だれ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 女の子が公園で遊んでいます。
example_sentences.english: A girl is playing in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 女[おんな]の子[こ]が公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]んでいます。

items.mnemonic_text: Power (力) worked in the rice field (田): a working man.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>rice field</radical> stretching out under the sun, and the one person out there doing the heavy lifting. He bends his arm, flexes his <radical>power</radical>, and drags the plow across the paddies all day. Someone with that much power working the rice field — that's the <kanji>man</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The man out in the field takes a break and starts pounding out a rhythm on his empty water bucket: <reading>だん</reading>, だん, だん. Every man on the trail can hear that drumbeat and grins.

example_sentences.japanese: あの男の人は誰ですか。
example_sentences.english: Who is that man over there?
example_sentences.furigana: あの男[おとこ]の人[ひと]は誰[だれ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 小さい男の子が犬を見ました。
example_sentences.english: A small boy saw a dog.
example_sentences.furigana: 小[ちい]さい男[おとこ]の子[こ]が犬[いぬ]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 男の人が部屋に入りました。
example_sentences.english: A man entered the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 男[おとこ]の人[ひと]が部屋[へや]に入[はい]りました。

items.mnemonic_text: A swaddled baby with arms out: a child.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at this character: it's a swaddled <radical>child</radical> with its little arms flung out to the sides. That bundled shape wriggling and reaching is exactly what this kanji is — a <kanji>child</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A child at the riverbank keeps splashing everyone, so you press a finger to your lips and go "<reading>し</reading>!" — the sound you make to shush a rowdy kid. That soft "し" is how you hush this child.
items.description: Means "child"; a very common kanji appearing in words for children and as a frequent name ending.

example_sentences.japanese: あの男の子は私の弟です。
example_sentences.english: That boy is my younger brother.
example_sentences.furigana: あの男[おとこ]の子[こ]は私[わたし]の弟[おとうと]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は新しい帽子を買いました。
example_sentences.english: She bought a new hat.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は新[あたら]しい帽[ぼう]子[し]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日、子供とお菓子を食べます。
example_sentences.english: I eat sweets with my child every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]、子[こ]供[ども]とお菓[か]子[し]を食[た]べます。

items.mnemonic_text: An upright frame with pupils inside: an eye.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A tall rectangle ruled into layers and stood on its end is an <kanji>eye</kanji> with the pupil drawn straight in.
items.reading_mnemonic: A woodcarver named <reading>もく</reading> is whittling a tiny wooden eye at Koichi's konbini counter, holding it up to inspect the grain. Every time he blinks, he mutters "もく, もく" as he lines the carving up with his own eye.
items.description: Count the bars inside the box. 目 is tall with two horizontals. 日 has one. 自 is 目 with a small slash added on top of the box.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女の目は大きいです。
example_sentences.english: Her eyes are big.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]の目[め]は大[おお]きいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 祖父は目が悪いです。
example_sentences.english: My grandfather has bad eyesight.
example_sentences.furigana: 祖[そ]父[ふ]は目[め]が悪[わる]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 自分の目で見ました。
example_sentences.english: I saw it with my own eyes.
example_sentences.furigana: 自[じ]分[ぶん]の目[め]で見[み]ました。

items.mnemonic_text: A dangling shape on the side of the head: an ear.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and you'll spot a dangling <radical>ear</radical> shape hanging off the side of a head. That soft, drooping flap catching every sound is an <kanji>ear</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A jittery DJ named Jiji cups a hand to his ear and shouts "<reading>じ</reading>, じ, do you hear that beat?" — the sound goes straight into his ear as じ.
items.description: Means "ear"; the body part, and shows up in words about hearing and listening.

example_sentences.japanese: あの犬は耳が大きいです。
example_sentences.english: That dog has big ears.
example_sentences.furigana: あの犬[いぬ]は耳[みみ]が大[おお]きいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんの耳は小さいです。
example_sentences.english: The baby's ears are small.
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]ちゃんの耳[みみ]は小[ちい]さいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 耳が冷たいです。
example_sentences.english: My ears are cold.
example_sentences.furigana: 耳[みみ]が冷[つめ]たいです。

items.mnemonic_text: An open square: a mouth.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character: it's just an open square, a hole with nothing inside. Picture it as a <radical>mouth</radical> hanging wide open, mid-yawn or mid-shout. An open square, an opening — a <kanji>mouth</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, leans across the beeping till and shouts an order to his stock boy, his mouth wide open: 「<reading>こう</reading>!」 Every time he barks like that, you picture that gaping mouth and hear こう.
items.description: Means "mouth" or "opening"; a common N5 kanji that shows up in words about mouths, entrances, and exits.

example_sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんの口は小さいです。
example_sentences.english: The baby's mouth is small.
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]ちゃんの口[くち]は小[ちい]さいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 出口はどこですか。
example_sentences.english: Where is the exit?
example_sentences.furigana: 出[で]口[ぐち]はどこですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行の窓口に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to the bank's service window.
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]の窓[まど]口[ぐち]に行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: Fingers and a wrist branching out: a hand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely and you can see the fingers spreading out from a <radical>hand</radical>'s wrist. That's the whole picture: fingers plus a wrist, held up for you to shake. It's a <kanji>hand</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A magician named Shu reaches out a bare hand and, with a flick, pulls a coin from behind your ear. As the coin lands in her palm she winks and says, "<reading>しゅ</reading>, that's all in the hand."
items.description: Means "hand"; a very common kanji that appears in everyday words for hands, gestures, and doing things by hand.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼の手は大きいです。
example_sentences.english: His hands are big.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]の手[て]は大[おお]きいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 母は料理が上手です。
example_sentences.english: My mother is good at cooking.
example_sentences.furigana: 母[はは]は料[りょう]理[り]が上手[じょうず]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 郵便局で切手を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a stamp at the post office.
example_sentences.furigana: 郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]で切[きっ]手[て]を買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth over stopping legs: a foot that carries you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> sits on top of a pair of legs. The legs have skidded to a halt — they are <radical>stopping</radical> hard. They end in one part: a <radical>foot</radical>. That's your <kanji>foot</kanji>, your leg, plenty to stand on.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker named Sok is nursing a blister on her foot. Every painful step she counts out loud, 「<reading>そく</reading>、そく、そく」, until she finally reaches the vending machine at the top and decides that's enough walking for one day.
items.description: Means foot, leg, or to suffice/be enough; shows up in words for body parts and in verbs about having sufficient amounts.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は足が長いです。
example_sentences.english: She has long legs.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は足[あし]が長[なが]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 足が冷たいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬は足が速いです。
